source.title: InfoBatch: Lossless Training Speed Up by Unbiased Dynamic Data Pruning
source.authors: Zi-Heng Qin; K. Wang; Zangwei Zheng; Jian-Yang Gu; Xiang Peng; Zhao-Pan Xu; Da-Quan Zhou; Lei Shang; Bai-Gui Sun; Xuan-Song Xie; Yang You

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: Tests held-out classification performance under dynamic data pruning, a training condition not covered by the listed versions.
record.gate_note: Reports test accuracy for natural-label training with and without data pruning. It does not measure training error, arbitrary-label memorization, or the train–test gap, and does not test any listed version directly.
record.test_reason: Table 7 bears on V4 despite being presented as an InfoBatch robustness evaluation: on CIFAR-10, ResNet-50 trained with SGD reaches 95.6% accuracy, versus 94.3% with AdamW and 95.0% with LAMB. The corresponding InfoBatch results preserve this ordering. Appendix A specifies individual learning rates rather than a broad tuning search. The pruning experiments otherwise test none of V1–V8.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes the authors' conclusion: InfoBatch achieves lossless acceleration across their evaluated tasks with reduced training cost and pruning overhead. Qualify this as applying to suitable pruning and annealing settings; aggressive pruning degrades accuracy, and the authors identify limited-epoch training as requiring further adaptation.
record.recipe_differences: Uses dynamic, probabilistic pruning of low-loss training samples, rescales retained losses, and returns to full-data training in the final epochs. The paper compares resulting test accuracy with full-data training.
record.method_sensitivity: Pruning ratio and annealing fraction affect performance: the text reports degraded performance when r ≥ 0.6 and lossless performance when δ ≤ 0.875 in the tested settings. Dataset, architecture, optimizer, and task are varied.

fits_no_version.finding: InfoBatch preserves or nearly preserves full-data accuracy in many tested settings, while higher pruning ratios can reduce accuracy. These are evaluations of the study's acceleration method.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dynamic probabilistic pruning with gradient rescaling and final full-data training can reduce training cost while approximately preserving held-out performance in the evaluated settings.

record.problems: The paper reports test accuracy but not training error or the train–test gap, so these results cannot establish how that gap changes. Some findings are figure-only and not extracted as numeric rows.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 comparisons for other pruning and coreset methods, Table 2 efficiency values, Table 4 ablations, Table 5 alternate pruning conditions, Table 8 diffusion FID, Table 9 instruction-tuning benchmark scores, Table 10 Tiny-ImageNet, and Table 12 same-compute full-dataset comparison were omitted because they concern pruning-method or task comparisons rather than the listed claim versions. Figure-only sweeps of r and δ were not assigned numeric values.

untested.parts: No fixed-random-label fitting or natural-versus-random-label held-out comparison.
No width sweep, interpolation threshold, or zero-training-error comparison.
No convolutional-versus-fully-connected comparison or local-connectivity intervention.
No training-performance comparison, broad hyperparameter search, Adam-to-SGD switching, coupled-versus-decoupled weight-decay intervention, or language-model optimizer comparison.
No controlled large-versus-small-batch held-out comparison. Discussion of large-batch training and use of LARS/LAMB do not supply one.
No dropout or joint dropout-and-weight-decay removal intervention.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measurement or ranking of generalization gaps.
No removal based on label-memorization influence scores. Loss, forgetting, EL2N, and generic influence-based pruning do not establish the specified memorization intervention.

record.verdict_notes: The record overlooks the cross-optimizer evidence in Table 7 and miscopies its AdamW values. V4 support is confined to the reported recipes: the paper does not document a systematic optimizer-tuning search or show whether training performance is matched. No train–test-gap measurement is needed to establish this held-out-performance comparison.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance under natural labels are not compared.
No network-width sweep or interpolation-threshold analysis.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
No adaptive-optimizer versus SGD generalization comparison.
No large-batch versus small-batch comparison under fixed epoch budgets.
No sharpness or other generalization-measure comparison.

rows.subject: ResNet-50

rows.note: Table 7 separately reports accuracy and saved cost.
rows.check: The extracted numbers are wrong: Table 7 reports AdamW full-data accuracy 94.3% and InfoBatch accuracy 94.4%, not 95.6% for both. Against SGD's 95.6%, the deficits are 1.3 and 1.2 percentage points. Table 7 names AdamW, while Appendix A calls the optimizer Adam when specifying learning rate 0.0006; retain this naming ambiguity.

relationships.condition: CIFAR-10 ResNet-50, full-data training, Table 7 recipes with specified learning rates
relationships.reason: R13, corrected R14, and R16 show SGD at 95.6%, AdamW at 94.3%, and LAMB at 95.0%; both tested adaptive optimizers have worse held-out accuracy under these recipes.
relationships.display_finding: Reported accuracy favors SGD over AdamW and LAMB under the specified recipes, but the comparison remains unverified.

relationships.display_finding: Reported accuracy still favors SGD over AdamW and LAMB with pruning, but the comparison remains unverified.
